events.context: User provides text about agent scaffolding capabilities and risks, including formal definitions and examples like MedBench and OpenClaw.
System extracts key actions and decisions: introduction of capabilities, expansion of attack surface, formal theorem on governance vs. capability, and specific cases.
Extracted capabilities: filesystem read/write, API credential storage, messaging integration, code execution, long-running processes.
Defined variables: C (capability), G (governance), R (risk). Conditions: G ≥ C improves safety, G < C amplifies risk.
MedBench demonstrates G ≥ C with safety gains; OpenClaw demonstrates G < C with vulnerabilities.
OpenClaw architecture includes agent scaffolding, tool access, API credentials, persistent runtime, network exposure, but lacks governance controls.
Attacker pipeline: input → compromised agent reasoning → unconstrained tool execution → system compromise.
Attacker capabilities: leak API credentials, expose communication histories, execute arbitrary commands, automate attacks, persist access.
Identified paradox: agent scaffolding improves safety with governance but is dangerous without it, due to capability amplification.
Derived design principle: agent capability must be matched by proportional governance mechanisms.
Required controls: capability-based permissions, runtime policy verification, network isolation, action auditing, constrained tool execution.
Without controls, agent scaffolding transforms model errors into system-level failures beyond traditional deployment risks.
